issues.legal_issue: A civil court may determine whether property is evacuee property when the Custodian never declared it to be evacuee property and no longer had authority to make that determination.
material_facts: The owner remained in India, personally managed the house, and collected rent until he left India for good in or after 1963.

No notification or other documentary evidence showed that the Custodian had declared the house evacuee property after an inquiry, or that proceedings to do so were pending when the relevant statutory restriction on new declarations took effect.
The civil suit required the court to determine whether the house had been evacuee property, and no order made by an authority under the evacuee-property legislation was being challenged.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s jurisdiction was not barred and it could determine whether the house was evacuee property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 7 and 8 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, a declaration following an inquiry is a prerequisite to vesting in the Custodian; Section 7A ended the power to make new declarations subject to its stated exceptions. Sections 28 and 46 do not bar a civil court from deciding a question that the Custodian never decided when the Custodian’s power to decide it has ended. Custodian of Evacuee Property, Punjab v. Jafran Begum was explained as barring civil-court jurisdiction where the Custodian had decided the question under Section 7, and Fazalbhoy v. Official Trustee of Maharashtra was cited on the need for a declaration for vesting.

rule.if: civil_title_suit and property_owner_remained_in_india_and_managed_property and no_custodian_declaration and no_pending_declaration_proceeding and custodian_power_had_ended

predicates.civil_title_suit: A party brought a civil suit in which determining whether property was evacuee property was necessary to resolve a claim to rights in that property.
predicates.property_owner_remained_in_india_and_man: The property owner remained in India while personally managing the property and collecting its rent.
predicates.no_custodian_declaration: The Custodian had not declared the property evacuee property after an inquiry.
predicates.no_pending_declaration_proceeding: No proceeding to declare the property evacuee property was pending when the relevant restriction on new declarations took effect.
predicates.custodian_power_had_ended: The Custodian no longer had authority to make a declaration concerning the property when the question came before the civil court.

issues.definition: When a civil title suit raises the status of property that its owner remained in India to manage, and the Custodian neither declared it nor had a pending proceeding or continuing power to declare it, the civil court may decide that status.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory sale from a rehabilitation compensation pool cannot transfer title to property that did not qualify as evacuee property and therefore could not lawfully enter the pool.
material_facts: The appellant relied on a sale by rehabilitation authorities and a sale certificate as the source of his title.
The house had never been declared evacuee property, and no applicable deeming basis established that it was evacuee property.
The record contained no evidence of the required acquisition notification, and the property therefore had not been shown to qualify for inclusion in the compensation pool.
issues.conclusion: The purported acquisition and sale could not lawfully place the house in the compensation pool or transfer title to the appellant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(c) of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 defines evacuee property by reference to property declared or deemed declared evacuee property under the 1950 Act. Under Section 12, only qualifying evacuee property may be acquired for the compensation pool; under Section 20, only property in that pool may be transferred. A property that does not satisfy the definition cannot lawfully be acquired for the pool or sold under Section 20.

predicates.statutory_compensation_pool_sale: A purchaser claims title under a sale by rehabilitation authorities of property purportedly transferred from a compensation pool.
predicates.property_not_declared_or_deemed_evacuee_: The property had neither been declared evacuee property nor been shown to qualify as evacuee property under an applicable deeming rule.

issues.definition: If a purchaser claims title through a compensation-pool sale but the property was not declared or deemed evacuee property, the sale cannot transfer title.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory finality of orders does not bar a civil court from considering a defense that a purported sale was outside the authority conferred by the governing legislation.
material_facts: The appellant, as plaintiff, relied on the purported sale to claim title.
The respondents resisted that claim by arguing that the sale was a nullity because the property had never been declared evacuee property and had never lawfully formed part of the compensation pool.
The respondents were not seeking to set aside the sale order as claimants; they raised its invalidity as a defense to the appellant’s suit.
issues.conclusion: The statutory finality provision did not bar the civil court from considering the respondents’ defense that the purported sale was a nullity.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27 of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954 gives finality to orders made by an officer or authority under that Act, but its words “under this Act” do not protect orders made outside the Act or in excess of jurisdiction. The Court distinguished Section 27 from the broader bar in Section 46 of the Administration of Evacuee Property Act, 1950, and held that N. S. Gujral v. Custodian of Evacuee Property did not apply because its facts were different.

predicates.civil_suit_to_enforce_purported_statutor: A purchaser brings a civil suit relying on a purported statutory sale to establish rights in property.
predicates.defendant_raises_invalidity_as_defense: The opposing party argues that the sale is invalid in order to resist the purchaser’s claim, rather than bringing a claim to set aside the sale order.
predicates.sale_outside_authority: The purported sale concerned property that did not qualify for transfer under the governing statutory scheme.

issues.definition: When a purchaser seeks to enforce a purported statutory sale in a civil suit, the defendant may raise as a defense that the sale was outside the authority granted by law.

issues.legal_issue: Property did not vest automatically in the Custodian under the former provincial ordinance when its owner remained in India until migrating to Pakistan years later.
material_facts: The owner remained in India until 1963 or later and personally managed the house and collected its rent during that period.
The owner migrated to Pakistan only after the former provincial ordinance had ceased to apply.
issues.conclusion: The house did not vest automatically in the Custodian under the former provincial ordinance.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the U.P. Ordinance No. 1 of 1949 did not apply because the owner remained in India until long after the ordinance ceased to operate; consequently, automatic vesting under that ordinance could not arise.

predicates.owner_remained_in_india_after_ordinance_: The property owner continued to reside in India after the former provincial ordinance ceased to apply.
predicates.owner_migrated_later: The property owner migrated to another country only after that ordinance had ceased to apply.

issues.definition: If the owner remained in India after the former ordinance ceased to apply and migrated only later, the property did not vest automatically under that ordinance.
